_note: The reviewer's lines (am_puck): names the guideline, why it matters, and what changed in the code.

lines.r0-hello: And I'm the reviewer. When something sounds wrong, I'll name the guideline it falls under, and explain why it matters to the person it stops. When it's fixed, I'll say what changed in the code.
lines.r0-first: This is a first pass, before testing with people with disabilities. It finds problems early, so they can be fixed, and so the time with people goes on what only they can tell us.
lines.r0-series: Each step gets its own short video. When we find a problem, we fix it, and test again in the same video. At the end, we list what still needs testing with people.
lines.r1-button: That's what a screen reader needs. Expanded, false, is announced as collapsed, so the person knows there's more behind it.
lines.r1-count: Hidden content should stay out of a screen reader's way. Nothing's wrong yet… but it's the first thing to listen for, in the reading pass.
lines.r2-skip: That's [WCAG](/wˈʌkæɡ/) two point four point one, Bypass Blocks. Without it, a keyboard user tabs through every link in the header, on every page.
lines.r2-focus: That's two point four point seven, Focus Visible. If you can't see where focus is, using a keyboard is guesswork.
lines.r2-close: Tab, Shift-Tab, Return, Escape, Space, and typing to choose. Every control works without a mouse, and focus is never trapped or lost. For what was tested, the goal of step two is met. [WCAG](/wˈʌkæɡ/) two point one point one, Keyboard, holds here.
lines.r3-sfy: A name, a role, and a state. That's what [WCAG](/wˈʌkæɡ/) four point one point two asks for.
lines.r3-why: There's no menu on screen. The settings panel is closed, but its four dropdowns are still reaching VoiceOver. That's a problem under [WCAG](/wˈʌkæɡ/) four point one point two, Name, Role, Value. If you're listening, it sounds like the page has stopped, right at the control that sets the site up for you.
lines.r3-fix: The fix: the panel is now left empty while it's closed. Here's the same page after that change.
lines.r3-holds: Four point one point two holds here.
lines.r4-headings: That's [WCAG](/wˈʌkæɡ/) one point three point one, Info and Relationships. Headings are how someone using a screen reader skims a page.
lines.r4-doubled: Each link still makes sense, so [WCAG](/wˈʌkæɡ/) two point four point four is met. But a list of links is how people scan a page, and this one takes several seconds per link. It's worth fixing.
lines.r4-fix: Two fixes. Each link is now described by its summary alone, and a small script makes Safari redraw whatever just lost focus. Here's the same list after both changes.
lines.r5-state: Name, role and state, all three. That's [WCAG](/wˈʌkæɡ/) four point one point two.
lines.r5-escape: Focus isn't lost. Where focus goes when a panel or a dialog closes is one of the most common keyboard problems, and here it's right.
lines.r6-stale: That seems to be VoiceOver in Safari, with a standard dropdown. It isn't the page.
lines.r6-note: That's a status message, and it's only on screen: it should be announced, without going to look. That's a problem under [WCAG](/wˈʌkæɡ/) four point one point three, Status Messages. Someone listening can't tell whether their choice worked.
lines.r6-fix: The fix: a status line that says what each change did. Here's the same task on the fixed version, the one that's live now.
lines.r6-holds: Four point one point three holds here.
lines.r8-why1: One more feature to test: Describe this page. A screen reader reads a page one item at a time, in a line. It doesn't say that the essays fill most of the page, or that a narrow column sits beside them.
lines.r8-why2: For someone who's blind, a picture of the layout is a map. It says what's on the page before reading all of it, and where things are when a sighted colleague says it's in the column on the right.
lines.r8-gap: What it says is useful. But on opening it only says its name, so someone has to explore to find out what the page is like. That's not a guideline failure, but it holds back the whole point of the feature.
lines.r8-fix: The fix, now live: the heading carries the description, so it's read the moment the dialog opens. Same steps, on the live site.
lines.r9-open: Last, what this first pass can't tell us. A screen reader shows whether things work as built, not whether they help the people they're for. These need people with disabilities, on their own devices and settings. I'll show each one on the page as we name it.
lines.r9-readers: Second, other screen readers and devices. We're back on the home page. This pass used VoiceOver in Safari only, and its biggest finding came from how Safari passes hidden content to VoiceOver. JAWS, NVDA, VoiceOver on iPhone and TalkBack all behave differently.
lines.r9-motion: Fourth, motion. Under the introduction, a band of drawings drifts slowly sideways, and thin lines and points move across the dark background behind the heading. A pause button sits beside Set for you. It works… but is it found in time, and is the motion comfortable before it is? People with vestibular disorders can tell us.
lines.r9-voice: Sixth, voice control and switch access. Names were checked for what a screen reader says, not for what people say aloud, and the home page has more than fifty stops for someone moving one step at a time.
lines.r9-close: The next test is with people.
lines.r8-review: Now the feature does its job from the first second. Whether the description helps is for blind people to tell us.
lines.r4-rings: That's [WCAG](/wˈʌkæɡ/) two point four point seven, Focus Visible. Someone who sees the screen while using VoiceOver, or a person sitting beside them, needs to find focus at a glance. The page's styles are right: this is a bug in Safari. But people still see it, so the page works around it.
